newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russians and Azeris up Caspian oil stakes.
newsitem.headline: Russians and Azeris up Caspian oil stakes.

text.p: Russian oil companies raised the stakes in the great Caspian energy game this week, signing two more big production sharing deals with Azerbaijan and holding talks with Azeri President Haydar Aliyev on strengthening ties.

Aliyev told reporters on Friday, the last day of a three-day official visit to Moscow, that developing huge Azeri oil and gas reserves was an economic priority for the former Soviet republic, and that Russian firms should have a major role.
"Today I spoke to representatives of (oil companies) YUKOS and SIDANKO and a number of other oil companies, and further talks will take place," he told a news conference.
Aliyev gave no further details of the talks, but was speaking in the context of Russian and other foreign oil firms developing Azerbaijan's massive offshore oil reserves.
YUKOS is Russia's second largest oil company by production and SIDANKO its fifth biggest.
Aliyev also brokered two off-shore oil exploration and production deals during his visit.
LUKoil, Russia's largest oil company, signed a $2-billion deal with Azerbaijan's state oil company SOCAR on Thursday to develop the Yalama oilfield.
LUKoil will get a 60 percent stake in the deal and SOCAR 40 percent. The Caspian field is estimated to contain around 50 million tonnes of oil.
SOCAR signed on Friday a $1-billion preliminary agreement with LUKoil and Russia's state oil company Rosneft to develop the Kyapaz oilfield.
SOCAR would get a 50 percent stake in the project, LUKoil 30 percent and Rosneft 20 percent. Kyapaz's estimated reserves are pegged at over 50 million tonnes.

Azerbaijan, one of the Caspian states most open to foreign investment, has now signed deals worth around $20 billion with foreign oil firms hungry to tap some of the world's richest oil and gas resources.
Finding partners to oil exploration and production has proved relatively easy for Azerbaijan since its independence from Moscow in 1991.
But like its Caspian neighbours, transporting that oil to world markets for hard cash remains Azerbaijan's biggest hurdle.

Aliyev said three or four new oil pipelines would eventually have to be built from the Caspian region to the Mediterranean and Black Seas to cope with ballooning production, mainly from Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan.

"The potential for oil production (in the Caspian) is huge. Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan are particularly rich, and need to get this oil to international markets," Aliyev said. "There may be three (new pipelines), or even a fourth eventually."

But two oil pipelines are already being renovated and the most pressing problem for Azerbaijan and its Western partners is to strike a deal on using an existing route linking Baku with Russia's Black Sea export outlet of Novorossiisk.

Azerbaijan's single biggest oil venture so far -- the $8-billion Azerbaijan International Operating Company (AIOC) -- plans to start producing from its massive Caspian deposits in August and to pump early oil along the pipeline in October.
The consortium is headed by an alliance of British Petroleum and Norway's Statoil.
But wrangling between Russia and its independence-minded region of Chechnya, through which the pipeline passes, has held up a final deal for months.
Aliyev said he expected a final commercial agreement between the three sides to be signed soon.

"It was decided that three companies -- Transneft, the Azeri state oil company and the Chechen oil company (YUNKO) would sign a commercial agreement on using the pipeline," he said. "This will be signed today, tomorrow, or the day after tomorrow."
Transneft is Russia's state-owned oil pipeline monopoly.
Signing the agreement by companies and not states appears to represent a workable compromise to avoid the thorny issue of sovereignty blocking the agreement further.
